title: Security review: Quantization Profiles change controls + audit logs (FalconBank)
summary: FalconBank security review focused on change control for the opt-in Quantization Profile Library. Customer asked how Redwood enforces RBAC for route-level enablement, what gets written to audit logs (fields, retention, export), whether quantization can be globally disabled, and how Redwood prevents silent profile changes. Redwood confirmed: (1) route-level toggles only (no default-on), (2) deterministic resolution with compatibility guardrails and safe fallback to baseline, (3) immutable, versioned profile IDs (with signing/integrity checks) and no silent upgrades when pinning a specific profile, (4) audit events with actor, route, before/after diff, and outcome (applied/fallback/disabled), (5) global kill-switch + per-tenant override option, and (6) Console change history view and API-driven configuration for internal approvals.
topics: RBAC model for who can enable quantization per route
Audit log event fields and export options (SIEM/Splunk)
Approval workflows and separation of duties
Deterministic profile selection, compatibility checks, and fallback behavior
Data handling: what metadata vs request content is logged
action_items: Redwood (Naomi Feldman): Send FalconBank the audit log event schema/field list for quantization profile changes, including example payloads (by 2025-03-14).
Redwood (Marcus Lin): Share Security FAQ addendum covering kill-switch behavior, per-tenant override, and retention defaults for audit logs (by 2025-03-14).
Redwood (Chloe Martin): Confirm current Console RBAC permissions required for route config changes and whether FalconBank can scope to a dedicated 'Route Admin' role (by 2025-03-18).
FalconBank (Priya Shah): Provide Redwood the target IAM model (SSO groups) and desired separation-of-duties policy for config changes (no date).
FalconBank (Tom Reyes): Identify 1–2 pilot routes/models for beta enablement and the internal approval path (no date).
next_steps: Redwood to follow up with audit log samples + RBAC matrix.
Schedule a 30-min working session with FalconBank IAM team to map SSO groups to Redwood roles.
If security review passes, start limited beta on one non-prod route with explicit rollback criteria.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: Mar 12, 2025
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 47 minutes
Title: Security review: Quantization Profiles change controls + audit logs (FalconBank)
Organizer: Miguel Santos (Redwood)

Attendees
Redwood: Miguel Santos (Enterprise Success), Naomi Feldman (Security & Compliance), Marcus Lin (Security Engineering), Chloe Martin (Console Backend)
FalconBank: Evan Brooks (Director, Cloud Security), Priya Shah (IAM Architect), Lena Hoffmann (GRC), Tom Reyes (ML Platform)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Customer asked about: RBAC, audit logs, approval workflows, rollback, and whether changes can be proven and exported.
- Redwood explained route-level enablement only, immutable profile versions, deterministic selection with compatibility checks, and a global kill-switch.


[00:00] Miguel Santos: Alright, I think we’re recording. Thanks everyone for the time. The goal today is really to walk through change controls around quantization profiles, how you turn it on per route, and then the audit and RBAC story.

[00:15] Evan Brooks: Great. Yeah, we’re evaluating Redwood for some workloads where cost is… not small. But we can’t accept “some engineer flipped a toggle and now the model behaves differently” without good controls.

[00:27] Miguel Santos: Totally. And to level set: in v1 it’s opt-in only. Default behavior remains unchanged if you do nothing.

[00:36] Tom Reyes: Can you define “toggle”? Is it tenant-wide or literally per endpoint?

[00:41] Chloe Martin: It’s per route. A route is the logical endpoint configuration in Redwood—model, limits, region policy, that kind of thing. Quantization is a field on the route config, so you can enable per route, and optionally scope by region or deployment tier if you’re using Dedicated.

[00:58] Priya Shah: Before we go too deep: who is allowed to do that? We use SSO groups, least privilege. Ideally only our platform team can do config changes.

[01:07] Naomi Feldman: Yep. We support SSO/SAML with group-to-role mapping. For the quantization setting specifically it’s not a “special hidden knob”—it’s governed by the same route-config write permission. In most customer setups that’s limited to org admins and a narrower “route admin” role.

[01:25] Priya Shah: Is it granular enough that someone can view but not edit? And can we separate “model catalog admin” from “route admin”?

[01:32] Naomi Feldman: View-only vs edit is supported. Separation between model catalog and route config depends on whether you’re using Hosted only or also Dedicated/Private features, but practically: the ability to publish profiles into the library is Redwood-controlled. Your team can only select from published, allowed profiles.

[01:52] Evan Brooks: That’s good. We want to avoid custom artifacts being uploaded from our side.

[01:58] Marcus Lin: Right, the profile artifacts are versioned and signed on our side in the model registry. The runtime checks integrity when loading. Customers don’t upload quantization kernels or weights here.

[02:12] Lena Hoffmann: When you say “signed,” do you have a paper trail? We’ll need evidence for change management.

[02:18] Marcus Lin: The signing is integrity—tamper detection—on the artifact blob. Separately we keep audit events for publish/deprecate actions internally, and for customer-visible events we log enable/disable and profile reference changes per route.

[02:35] Evan Brooks: Let’s talk audit logs. What exactly is logged when someone changes a route to enable quantization?

[02:42] Chloe Martin: When a route setting is changed via Console or API, we emit an audit event. It includes: actor (user id, email if available), org/tenant id, route id, route name, the field changes (before/after), timestamp, source (console/api), and a request id / correlation id.

[03:02] Chloe Martin: For quantization specifically we log the quant_profile_ref that was set. That resolves to a quant_profile_id once applied.

[03:12] Evan Brooks: “Resolves” meaning you allow aliases like “recommended” that can change underneath us?

[03:18] Miguel Santos: Good question. We debated that a lot. In GA we’re steering customers to pin an explicit versioned profile id. There are aliases in the system, but for security-sensitive accounts we can disable alias selection in Console and require explicit versions.

[03:35] Priya Shah: That’s important. We don’t want silent changes.

[03:38] Naomi Feldman: To be precise: if you pin a concrete profile version, it will not change unless you change it. If you choose an alias like “latest” then yes, by definition it could point to a newer version later. We can restrict that, and we also show warnings in Console when an alias is selected.

[03:58] Lena Hoffmann: If a newer version is published, do you notify customers?

[04:03] Miguel Santos: For beta, it’s manual + release notes, and for GA we’re building a cadence/notification feed. But again, pinned versions don’t update automatically.

[04:15] Tom Reyes: When the request runs, do we know whether quantization was actually applied? Like if it falls back.

[04:21] Marcus Lin: Yes. The runtime annotates logs and traces with a quant_profile_id and a resolution outcome: applied, fallback, or disabled.

[04:31] Evan Brooks: And fallback triggers are… what? Like incompatible GPU?

[04:35] Marcus Lin: Exactly. Compatibility checks happen in policy evaluation before the request hits the runtime. We check model variant, GPU sku class, max context/sequence length constraints, and a few “known caveats” fields. If it’s incompatible, we deterministically fall back to baseline precision.

[04:55] Tom Reyes: Deterministically meaning every time the same route, same region, same hardware, same input shape… you’ll pick the same profile.

[05:03] Marcus Lin: Right. Same resolved policy yields same profile selection. We’re careful about “random kernel selection” kind of behavior.

[05:13] Evan Brooks: Where is that decision recorded? Like can we audit “it fell back” events.

[05:19] Chloe Martin: We have metrics and logs. For audit logs, we log config changes. For “runtime applied fallback,” that’s operational telemetry: metrics like fallback_rate and request-level logs with the outcome. Those can be exported through your usual log pipeline.

[05:38] Priya Shah: Do you support exporting audit logs to Splunk? We’re a Splunk shop.

[05:42] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We have a few options depending on deployment: (1) API to pull audit events; (2) streaming export to your SIEM via our audit log exporter integration; (3) for Private/VPC deployments we can also ship to your collector endpoint. We can align on Splunk HEC vs S3 bucket ingestion.

[06:07] Lena Hoffmann: Retention period?

[06:10] Naomi Feldman: Default retention in the platform is 90 days for audit logs, and for enterprise we can extend. For Private it depends on your configured storage. We can put it in the contract addendum if you need 1 year.

[06:25] Evan Brooks: Okay. Another thing: approval workflows. We require two-person approval for production config changes. Do you have that natively?

[06:33] Chloe Martin: Not as a first-class “four-eyes approval” inside the Console today. What we support is: restrict who can edit, and everything is API-driven so you can implement your approval flow in your internal tooling—like ServiceNow—then call the route config API with a service token tied to an approved pipeline.

[06:56] Priya Shah: So basically, integrate with our CI/CD for config. That can work. But we need to ensure no one can bypass the pipeline through the UI.

[07:05] Naomi Feldman: That’s where RBAC helps. We can set it up so only a small break-glass group has UI write permissions. Everyone else is view-only.

[07:16] Evan Brooks: Break-glass is fine as long as it’s audited.

[07:18] Naomi Feldman: It is. The audit entry includes actor identity, and we can enable extra “reason for change” prompts in Console for certain sensitive fields. It’s not perfect, but it’s there.

[07:34] Tom Reyes: For Dedicated, does the route config apply across all regions or per region?

[07:39] Chloe Martin: Route config can be global, and you can override per region. Quantization profile enablement supports that same mechanism. The audit log will include what scope you changed.

[07:52] Evan Brooks: Let’s talk rollback. If we enable quantization and something looks off, what’s the fastest way to revert?

[07:59] Miguel Santos: Fastest is disable on the route. That’s immediate once propagated.

[08:04] Marcus Lin: There’s also a global kill-switch on our side, and we can expose a tenant-level disable. The kill-switch is for emergencies—if we see systemic regressions, we can force baseline everywhere even if routes are configured.

[08:19] Evan Brooks: Can we control that kill-switch? Or is that Redwood-only?

[08:24] Naomi Feldman: The platform-wide kill-switch is Redwood-controlled. For customers with stricter requirements we can enable a tenant-level override where your org admin can disable quantization across your tenant regardless of route settings. That gives you an “off everywhere” button.

[08:44] Priya Shah: That’s what we’d want. One click, and we’re back to baseline.

[08:49] Tom Reyes: When you disable, do you flush KV cache or anything? I’m thinking about weird behavior where cached prefix is from different precision.

[08:57] Marcus Lin: Good call. We keep KV cache keyed by model version and quantization mode so we don’t mix. Switching modes causes cache miss, not cross-contamination. There can be a perf effect, but not correctness drift from mixing caches.

[09:16] Tom Reyes: Okay.

[09:18] Lena Hoffmann: Do audit logs include prompts or outputs? We’re sensitive.

[09:22] Naomi Feldman: Audit logs do not include request payloads. They include metadata about config changes. Request logs/traces can include request ids and timing, but content logging is configurable, and for most enterprise customers it’s disabled by default.

[09:38] Evan Brooks: Good.

[09:40] Priya Shah: How do you prevent an engineer from enabling an incompatible profile? Like picking INT8 on a GPU that doesn’t support it.

[09:47] Chloe Martin: The Console and API do validation before saving, and the policy engine does validation at resolve-time. If you try to set something incompatible, the API returns a structured error with remediation suggestions. If it passes config-time but later becomes incompatible due to environment changes, we fall back at runtime and emit fallback telemetry.

[10:12] Evan Brooks: Environment changes meaning you moved capacity to a different GPU?

[10:16] Miguel Santos: Or a region where Dedicated has different SKU, yes.

[10:20] Evan Brooks: Okay. Do you block the change, or allow and fallback?

[10:24] Marcus Lin: We do both depending on certainty. If we know at config-time it’s incompatible with your declared deployment tier/region, we block. If it’s a dynamic condition at request-time, we fallback.

[10:40] Tom Reyes: Is fallback silent?

[10:43] Marcus Lin: Not silent. It’s observable: metrics, logs, trace annotations. You can alert on fallback_rate.

[10:50] Evan Brooks: Do you have recommended thresholds?

[10:52] Miguel Santos: Our SRE team typically flags sustained fallback_rate above 1–2% for a route, but we tune it by volume. We can share what we use internally.

[11:05] Lena Hoffmann: For compliance, we need an audit trail of who changed what and when, and ideally the diff.

[11:11] Chloe Martin: The audit event includes a diff of the route config fields that changed. In Console there’s also a change history view. You can filter by route and see “quantization_profile_ref: default -> qp_foo_v3” and the actor.

[11:28] Priya Shah: Are those audit logs immutable?

[11:31] Naomi Feldman: The audit log store is append-only; admins can’t edit past events. For exports, once it’s in your SIEM you have your own immutability controls.

[11:43] Evan Brooks: Okay. One more: We care about separation between Redwood staff and our data. If Redwood can flip kill-switches, can Redwood also change our routes?

[11:53] Naomi Feldman: By default, Redwood employees do not have access to your Console or config. Support access is gated and time-bound with approvals. And for Private deployments you control that entirely.

[12:08] Evan Brooks: We’d want that documented.

[12:10] Miguel Santos: Yep, we can send our support access policy.

[12:14] Tom Reyes: On the quant profile library itself: how do you decide what’s “approved”? Like, can you publish experimental profiles?

[12:22] Marcus Lin: Profiles have status and metadata: experimental, stable, deprecated. Only stable profiles are shown by default. Experimental can be allowlisted per tenant.

[12:35] Tom Reyes: And quality evals?

[12:37] Miguel Santos: Applied ML runs regression suites and we have thresholds. If a profile regresses beyond threshold, it’s blocked or rolled back.

[12:49] Evan Brooks: That’s more of product, but relevant from risk.

[12:52] Lena Hoffmann: For risk, do you have an incident process if a profile causes issues?

[12:57] Naomi Feldman: Yes, standard incident management, plus for this feature we added specific rollback runbooks and a global disable mechanism.

[13:08] Priya Shah: Authentication: The API token used to change routes—can it be scoped to only specific routes?

[13:15] Chloe Martin: Scoped tokens can be limited to a project and specific resource types. Route-level scoping is on our roadmap; today it’s generally scoped by environment/project. But you can create separate projects per app and limit tokens accordingly.

[13:34] Evan Brooks: Noted. That might be a gap, but maybe manageable.

[13:38] Miguel Santos: We can also pair that with SSO group-based controls in the Console.

[13:45] Tom Reyes: If we run a canary, can we do 1% traffic to quant and 99% baseline?

[13:51] Chloe Martin: The route-level toggle is binary, but you can create two routes and split traffic on your side, or use our rollout policies if you’re using the advanced routing features. For beta we typically recommend route cloning: baseline route and quant route.

[14:12] Evan Brooks: And the audit logs show both routes are configured differently.

[14:15] Chloe Martin: Correct.

[14:17] Lena Hoffmann: I’m going to ask a boring GRC question: do you have SOC 2 and does it cover change management?

[14:23] Naomi Feldman: Yes, we’re SOC 2 Type II. Change management controls are included. We can share the report under NDA.

[14:31] Evan Brooks: Okay.

[14:33] Priya Shah: Let’s get concrete. What are the exact fields you log? We’ll need them for our control mapping.

[14:40] Chloe Martin: I’ll send an example, but verbally: event_type, event_id, occurred_at, actor_type (user/service), actor_id, actor_email (if user), ip_address, org_id, project_id, route_id, route_name, change_set (field path + old/new), and a request_id.

[15:03] Priya Shah: IP address is important.

[15:05] Chloe Martin: Yep, we capture it for Console actions and API calls where available.

[15:11] Evan Brooks: Do you log MFA status or SSO session info?

[15:16] Naomi Feldman: Not currently in the audit event, but authentication is via SSO and we can provide SSO enforcement docs. We can also add it as a request for the audit exporter if it’s required.

[15:32] Evan Brooks: Okay.

[15:34] Tom Reyes: For the runtime trace annotation: can we query by request id and see which profile was used?

[15:40] Marcus Lin: Yes. There’s a quant_profile_id field and an outcome field. Support can also help you look it up if you provide request id.

[15:49] Evan Brooks: But support access is gated.

[15:51] Marcus Lin: Correct.

[15:53] Lena Hoffmann: How quickly does a route config change propagate? We have concerns about “in-flight” requests.

[16:00] Marcus Lin: Usually within seconds to a minute depending on region. In-flight requests continue on the previous resolved policy; new requests pick up the new config. There’s no partial application within a single request.

[16:18] Priya Shah: And the system is deterministic across deployments? Hosted vs Dedicated.

[16:23] Miguel Santos: Same control plane, same schema. For Private, you run it in your environment but the behavior’s the same.

[16:31] Evan Brooks: Alright. This is mostly good. The main open item for me is: can we enforce “no alias,” pinned versions only, and can we have a tenant-wide off switch.

[16:44] Naomi Feldman: Both are doable. We’ll confirm with product what’s already supported vs needs enablement for your tenant. But the direction is yes.

[16:54] Chloe Martin: On alias: we can hide alias options in the Console for your org. On the API side, we can reject non-versioned refs for your tenant.

[17:05] Evan Brooks: Great.

[17:07] Tom Reyes: If we want to do a pilot, what’s the recommended approach for safety?

[17:12] Miguel Santos: Start on a non-prod route, pin a stable profile version, set up dashboards for latency/cost/fallback, then canary by routing a small subset of app traffic. Have rollback criteria. We’ll provide a playbook.

[17:30] Lena Hoffmann: And we’ll want the audit log export configured before any production trial.

[17:34] Miguel Santos: Makes sense.

[17:36] (crosstalk)

[17:37] Priya Shah: Sorry—one more thing. Can we get change history from the Console via API? For evidence collection.

[17:44] Chloe Martin: Yes. There’s an endpoint to list audit events and another for route change history, depending on what you prefer. We can walk your team through it.

[17:56] Evan Brooks: Okay. I think that covers it.

[18:00] Miguel Santos: Cool, let me recap next steps before we drop.

[18:04] Miguel Santos: Redwood will send (1) audit event schema and sample entries for route-level quantization changes, (2) a short doc on kill-switch and tenant override, and (3) RBAC matrix for who can edit routes. And we’ll schedule a working session with Priya’s team to map SSO groups.

[18:24] Evan Brooks: Sounds good.

[18:26] Lena Hoffmann: Thanks.

[18:27] Tom Reyes: Thanks everyone.

[18:29] Miguel Santos: Thanks all. End recording.

(Transcript ends)
